name: Lipodissolve (phosphatidylcholine injections)

lead: Lipodissolve, also called injection lipolysis, is a cosmetic procedure in which a mixture of phosphatidylcholine and the detergent sodium deoxycholate is injected into small pockets of fat. Practitioners who offer it say it shrinks localized fat and tightens skin, and it was marketed in the 2000s as a non-surgical alternative to liposuction.

Published support consists mostly of practitioner-authored reports and small studies. Reviews describe it as having drawn scrutiny from the media and the US Food and Drug Administration. A different deoxycholic-acid-only product, Kybella, was later approved by the FDA for fat under the chin, but that approval does not cover phosphatidylcholine mixtures.

paras: Proponents proposed that phosphatidylcholine breaks down fat, while later reviews suggest the deoxycholate detergent action, which destroys fat cell membranes, may account for observed effects. The body then clears the released material over weeks.

Reported problems include pain, bruising, swelling, nodules, severe inflammation and infection, including a published case of mycobacterial infection after injections. Mixtures are often compounded rather than manufactured to an approved standard. The FDA has not approved phosphatidylcholine injections for fat reduction.

lead: Lipodissolve, also known as injection lipolysis or PC/DC injection, is a cosmetic procedure in which a mixture of phosphatidylcholine (PC) and sodium deoxycholate (DC) is injected into subcutaneous fat with the aim of reducing small localized deposits. It belongs to the broader family of mesotherapy techniques, in which substances are injected into or just beneath the skin.[1][2]

Practitioners who developed the technique reported that it reduces localized fat and causes some skin retraction, and described it as an adjunct to or alternative to liposuction for patients seeking a minimally invasive option.[3] Reviews published in the late 2000s and early 2010s described the approach as having been received with initial enthusiasm and then critical scrutiny from the media and the US Food and Drug Administration.[4] The mesotherapy literature more broadly has been described by Wikipedia's summary of it as having limited scientific backing.[2]

Published human evidence consists mainly of practitioner case series and small studies, and at least one registered trial was terminated early.[5][6] The FDA approved a purified deoxycholic acid product, Kybella, for fat beneath the chin in 2015, which is a distinct product from phosphatidylcholine mixtures.[7]
infobox: Deoxycholic acid (Kybella), FDA-approved 2015 for submental fat
No FDA approval for phosphatidylcholine fat injections

paras: In the procedure, a practitioner injects a compounded solution containing phosphatidylcholine and the bile-salt detergent sodium deoxycholate into small areas of fat, such as under the chin, the abdomen, flanks or thighs, in a series of sessions. Practitioner publications from the 2000s described indications, expected after-effects such as swelling and tenderness, and the need for correct formula, technique and patient selection.[1][3]

The term lipodissolve was widely used in spas and aesthetic clinics in the 2000s, and the technique was sometimes offered under the heading of mesotherapy, a French-originated practice of multiple small injections that the Wikipedia article on the subject credits to Michel Pistor in the 1950s.[2]

Early proponents attributed fat loss to phosphatidylcholine itself. Later discussion in the literature suggests that deoxycholate, a detergent, destroys the membranes of fat cells and may explain the observed clinical effects.[2][7] Wikipedia's article on deoxycholic acid describes the purified compound as destroying fat cells in the treated area, with the body clearing the debris over several months.[7]

Authors who practice the technique report that it reduces small localized fat deposits and tightens skin in areas with small amounts of fat, cellulite or post-liposuction irregularities, while stating that it does not replace traditional liposuction and that outcomes depend on formula, injection technique and patient selection.[1] A paper on practice standards likewise described the procedure as growing quickly and argued that standards on indications, contraindications and acceptable post-injection effects were needed.[3]

A review of injectable fat-reduction therapies noted that these methods had faced critical scrutiny from the media and the FDA after initial enthusiasm, and that several new agents with detergent and lipolytic activity were then in development.[4] A 2012 journal article examined safety, effectiveness and patient satisfaction with lipodissolve for body sculpting.[8] Independent controlled evidence is limited, and Wikipedia's mesotherapy article states that cosmetic mesotherapy has not been tested in standard clinical trials.[2]

Expected short-term effects described by practitioners include swelling, bruising and tenderness.[3] More serious events are described in case reports. A 2022 case report in a dermatopathology journal described painful purulent nodules caused by Mycobacterium at the sites of lipodissolve injections.[9] Wikipedia's mesotherapy article also records that Australian health officials investigated a salon in 2008 after clients developed skin abscesses, one involving a mycobacterial infection, and quotes a dermatologist describing phosphatidylcholine as unpredictable and capable of causing severe inflammation at injection sites.[2]

Authorities have taken different positions on mesotherapy for fat. According to Wikipedia, France published a ban in 2011 that its Council of State later cancelled the same year on the basis that problems stemmed from unhygienic conditions, and Brazil and some other South American countries have banned the practice; in the US, the practice of injecting mixtures falls under state medical boards.[2]

Registered trials are small. A 2008 study of injection lipolysis to reduce abdominal subcutaneous fat enrolled 20 participants and is listed as completed.[5] A 2009 study of subcutaneous phosphatidylcholine and deoxycholate injections for localized fat removal enrolled 18 participants and was terminated.[6] Results of these registrations are not summarized in the registry entries cited here.

Published clinical literature otherwise consists of practitioner reports and reviews, such as a 2005 report of fat reduction and skin retraction and a 2011 review of injectables in development.[1][4] For the distinct deoxycholic-acid-only product Kybella, the FDA approval of 2015 was based on a phase III program, as summarized by Wikipedia.[2][7]

Lipodissolve was promoted in the 2000s as a lunchtime, non-surgical alternative to liposuction and appears in aesthetic-medicine discussion of body contouring. After scrutiny by regulators and the media, interest shifted to products with regulatory approval, notably deoxycholic acid for submental fat, approved by the FDA on April 29, 2015 per Wikipedia.[4][7]
Within looksmaxxing communities, injectable fat dissolvers are discussed mainly as a way to reduce submental fullness or facial fat, alongside approved options.

lore.intro: Fat-dissolving injections are discussed in appearance forums as a non-surgical option for chin and body fat, often with disagreement about product quality and safety.

timeline.event: The term mesotherapy is coined in the French press, according to Wikipedia.[2]
A practitioner report describes lipodissolve for localized fat reduction and skin retraction.[1]
A practice-standards paper describes rapid growth of PC/DC injection lipolysis; an Australian salon is investigated after skin abscesses.[2][3]
Review notes media and FDA scrutiny of injection lipolysis methods.[4]
The FDA approves deoxycholic acid (Kybella) for submental fat.[7]
Case report of mycobacterial nodules after lipodissolve injections.[9]
